title: Monsieur Ibrahim
full_review:
A young Jewish boy abandoned by his father finds an unlikely surrogate in an elderly Muslim grocer in the tender coming-of-age drama "Monsieur Ibrahim" (Sony Classics).

Buttressed by nuanced performances from both ends of the life spectrum, director Francois Dupeyron's intimate film is a poignant, though minor, fairy tale about love, loss, friendship and tolerance.

Set in Paris in the early 1960s, the story centers on Momo (Pierre Boulanger), a solitary 16-year-old living in a working-class neighborhood with his dyspeptic father (Gilbert Melki). Years earlier his mother and older brother (who may or not really exist) flew the coop, leaving Momo to his own devices while his father is at work. Like most boys his age, he spends his days blaring American rock 'n' roll music on the radio and fantasizing about girls. Full of adolescent insecurity, he can't work up the nerve to talk to the pretty red-haired beauty downstairs. Instead, without any parental figure to turn to for guidance or direction, Momo relieves his pubescent pangs by visiting a sympathetic prostitute.

Omar Sharif plays the eponymous Ibrahim, a paternal greengrocer who befriends the wayward youth. Having lost his wife long ago, Ibrahim, a member of the mystical branch of Islam known as Sufism, shares in Momo's inner isolation. Turning a blind eye to the boy's shoplifting, the Quran-quoting storekeeper tells Momo, "If you steal, I prefer you do it in my shop." They begin an intergenerational friendship, discussing life, love and movies, while filling each other's emotional emptiness.

When Momo's father follows his wife's lead out the door, Ibrahim is only too willing to adopt the boy as his own son. Their inner journey of self-discovery becomes an outer odyssey, as they travel to Turkey, Ibrahim's ancestral homeland, and toward the film's bittersweet climax.

Sharif brings a stately wintriness to the titular role, leavened by a soulful placidity that comes with the wisdom and detachment of age. Boulanger, conversely, is all energy, harnessing it one moment into the elation of puppy love, and exploding the next in a burst of adolescent rage. When Momo discovers that his father has deserted him, Boulanger's youthful elan is channeled into a shot of him crushing a felt hat, which is at once both violent and heartbreaking.

Some viewers will undoubtedly find the scenes involving Momo's deflowering by a prostitute troubling, to say the least, especially given the boy's age. Such valid concerns may be compounded by the devoutly religious Ibrahim's wink-wink nod of approval. However, without justifying such actions, Momo's love-starved attempts at affection should be judged in the context of his overwhelming loneliness.

His bordello encounters are less about sex than they are about a hunger for human tenderness and a thirst for interpersonal contact. The scent of innocence that perfumes these scenes is nowhere more evident than when Momo offers his threadbare teddy bear -- an archetypal symbol of childhood -- to one of the trollops in return for her kindness.

Without ever resorting to mawkish sentimentality, the film imparts a positive message about tolerance and mutual respect between people of different ages, cultures and faith traditions, denouncing as a "disease" any way of thinking that fosters divisiveness and bigotry. Ibrahim's pearls of wisdom are offered freely and, though filtered through his Islamic sensibilities, never come across as attempts to proselytize his secular Jewish charge. In fact, Ibrahim goes to great lengths to impress upon Momo his deep reverence for Judaism, as well as Christianity, taking the boy to Greek Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches as well as taking him to see whirling dervishes perform a Sufi ritual dance. While some may view this syncretism with suspicion, others may see it as a celebration of man's collective quest for God.

In one of the film's more touching moments, Ibrahim offers Momo some fatherly advice: "What you give is yours forever; what you keep is lost forever" -- a profound insight which should resonate deeply with Christians. At its core "Monsieur Ibrahim" is a story about hope and beauty. Quoting his holy book, the sage-like Ibrahim says, "You can find beauty wherever you look." Pope John Paul II echoes this when he writes, "The world will be saved by beauty." If so, perhaps this small film will play a modest part in that salvific process. Given the long, bloody history of Jewish-Muslim relations, let us pray that the spirit of harmony and shared humanity which permeates this movie is more than just a poet's -- or filmmaker's -- dream.

Subtitles.

Due to a few sexual encounters involving the teen protagonist and a prostitute, as well as sporadic crude expressions, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
